turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning, Mr Adams. You're booked for a check-up, ja?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, doc. The wife made the booking. I'm fine, it's just a check-up.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): How old are you now?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Sixty-four. March. Still in the garden, still walking the dog. Nothing wrong with me.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any worries, or purely routine?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Routine. The blood pressure, I suppose. That's the only thing I've got.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have you had the high blood pressure?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Five years... no, hang on. It was already there when I turned fifty, so that's fourteen years. They just fuss more now.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fourteen years. Which tablet are you on?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine. Five milligrams in the morning... no, sorry, ten. They bumped me to ten at the day hospital last year.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Amlodipine ten milligrams, once every morning. Anything else from the chemist?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Disprin. The aspirin. The seventy-five... ag, I checked the box this morning, it's the hundred milligram ones.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hundred milligrams. Do you take that every day?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm supposed to. I take it on and off, when I remember. Doesn't feel like it does anything.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): So not daily. Any cholesterol tablets, or anything for diabetes?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't have sugar. I don't like pills.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. Never swelled up or came out in a rash.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never been cut open.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? Shortness of breath?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Chest pain? No. I'm not that guy.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not when you walk, or on the stairs?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, you get a bit puffed at my age. It's not pain. I wouldn't even—
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Wouldn't even what?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Wouldn't have brought it up. It's a tight feeling, that's all, and only if I push it.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tight where, exactly?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Across the chest, and it's gone in about a minute if I slow down. We're on the third floor in Glenwood and the lift's out half the time, so it's the stairs or a fast walk to the Spar, and I still say it's nothing.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gone after how long, did you say?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): A minute. Maybe less. I stand on the landing and then I carry on.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did this tightness start?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Eish. It's not like I wrote it on the calendar.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Roughly, though. Days, or longer?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't put a date on it. Maybe a month. Could be more. I wasn't watching.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it come when you're sitting still, watching the rugby?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Only if I'm rushing. Slow and steady, nothing at all.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it go down the arm, or into the jaw?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I keep telling you, it's not heart pain.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sweating when it happens?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): And nausea, feeling sick with it?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose, sometimes, not really.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll leave the nausea as a maybe, not a yes and not a no. Any palpitations, the heart racing or thumping?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ever blacked out, or felt you might faint?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cough, phlegm, wheeze?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. The chest is fine apart from that stupid tight thing, which is nothing.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ankles puffy by the evening?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Shoes fit the same. Listen, the dog's in the bakkie and it's getting warm out there.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll keep it moving. Do you smoke?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Never have. A beer at the Saturday braai, two if the Boks are playing. That's my lot.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): And work?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Panel beater, retired three years. Now it's the garden, the dog, and those stairs. My wife drives and she booked this, she'll fetch me just now.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): In the family, heart attacks or strokes?
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): My dad had a heart attack, he was seventy... no, seventy-two, and he smoked his whole life. My mother had diabetes and she went at eighty. No strokes that I know of.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure today is one hundred and forty-eight over ninety-two. Higher than I want on ten milligrams.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this room. At the chemist last week it was one thirty something. Fine.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is seventy-eight and regular. Oxygen saturation ninety-eight percent.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lungs are clear, no crackles. Heart sounds are normal, no murmur. No swelling at the ankles.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): There you go. I'm alright. Can I head?

[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back: you came for a check-up, you said no to chest pain, and then you described a tight band across the chest on the stairs or fast walking, gone in about a minute if you stop, not while sitting and not down the arm. Amlodipine ten every morning, aspirin a hundred only on and off, and you can't date when it started.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. And it's mild. I'd still call this a check-up.

[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thinking out loud, I am not stamping a diagnosis this morning: that pattern can be angina, the heart short of blood on effort, or acid if you eat and then climb, or the chest muscles from the stairs. I am not calling this a heart attack.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Angina is a hell of a word for—

[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): For a tight feeling, I heard you. It's one possibility, not a label. A resting ECG can be normal and you can still have angina, so the tracing won't finish the question by itself.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): So what are you actually doing, then?
[SEG0068] person_1 (DOCTOR): An ECG today, and bloods for cholesterol, blood sugar and kidney function. Both before you go. Twenty minutes, window down, shade side, the dog will live.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. If you insist.
[SEG0070] person_1 (DOCTOR): The aspirin you were told to take is a hundred milligrams every day, with food. I'd like you to take it daily, not only when it crosses your mind.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, I'll try. No promises if I'm out on the boat.
[SEG0072] person_1 (DOCTOR): And when the tightness starts, you stop. Don't push on up the stairs. Wait until it passes.
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): I already do that.
[SEG0074] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it starts while you're sitting still, or you get a cold sweat, or you feel you might pass out, go to casualty or call an ambulance. Don't drive yourself.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): My wife can drive. Government casualty, though. Eish, the queue.
[SEG0076] person_1 (DOCTOR): Whichever is closest. Don't wait it out at home. And I'll see you here in a week for the results. That's a booked visit.
[SEG0077] person_2 (PATIENT): If the ECG is normal and the bloods are normal, we're finished, right?
[SEG0078] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not necessarily. If the story hasn't changed we might still talk about a stress test later. I'm not ordering that today, and I won't choose a cause until these are back.
[SEG0079] person_2 (PATIENT): So you don't know. You're leaving the blood pressure tablet alone?

[SEG0080] person_1 (DOCTOR): I don't know yet: possible angina stays on the list with reflux and a muscle strain, and I'm not choosing between them this morning. Keep the amlodipine at ten milligrams every morning, because one reading in here isn't enough to add another tablet. If the chemist numbers are up as well we handle that at the week visit, so bring the slip if your wife has it.
[SEG0081] person_2 (PATIENT): She keeps the papers. I still say it's nothing. Reception can point me, I know the passage.

spec.situation: Man or woman 50-70 who comes 'for a check-up' and only slowly admits a tight feeling in the chest when climbing stairs or walking fast; first denies chest pain, later describes the tightness. Takes a BP tablet and aspirin on and off. Doctor orders ECG and bloods.
features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

omissions.text: Nausea with the chest tightness was equivocal/uncertain ('sometimes, not really'); it was neither clearly present nor clearly absent.
Shortness of breath was specifically asked about and not clearly denied: patient said he gets 'a bit puffed' with exertion/at his age rather than giving a clear no.
No wheeze/phlegm was asked and answered negative as part of 'Cough, phlegm, wheeze?' / 'No cough. The chest is fine apart from that stupid tight thing'.
Family history detail missing: father's myocardial infarction was at age 72, and patient reported no known family history of stroke.
Doctor noted that a resting ECG can be normal and the patient can still have angina, so the ECG alone will not settle the question.
Possible future plan omitted: if symptoms/story persist despite normal ECG and bloods, they might still discuss a stress test later; not ordered today.
